options: Increments n once a second and clears the interval on unmount
Increments n once a second but leaves the interval running on unmount
Increments n once, because the dependency array is empty
Stops at 1, because the interval captured n = 0
rewrite.hint: Two details decide this: the empty dependency array and the p => p + 1 form of the update. Work out what each one prevents.
rewrite.explanation: The effect runs once after mount, starts the interval and returns a cleanup, so the timer is cleared when App unmounts and on Strict Mode's development remount. Writing the update as p => p + 1 means the callback never needs the n captured when the effect ran, so the counter keeps climbing; setN(n + 1) with an empty dependency array would stick at 1. The empty array is also what keeps one interval instead of restarting a new one on every render.

rationale: A good mastery-level composite: cleanup, empty dependencies and a functional update in twelve lines, correctly keyed. The rewrite turns the three dead options into the three bugs this code avoids, which is what makes the trace worth doing.

options: Once after mount, then never again
After every render, because setItems causes one
Only when items changes

rewrite.hint: Look at the second argument to useEffect and decide what it tells React about running the body again.
rewrite.explanation: An empty dependency array tells React there is nothing to watch, so the body runs after the first render and never again: one request goes out and setItems puts the JSON into state. Drop the array and every state update would re-run the effect, which is the refetch loop option two describes. Two caveats belong with this pattern: in development Strict Mode mounts the component twice, so you will see two requests, and with no cleanup a response that arrives after unmount or after a newer request still lands in state.

rationale: The most common data-loading shape in React and correctly keyed for production, but the item asserts 'once' without the Strict Mode caveat a learner will immediately observe in dev. The rewrite keeps the objective, wraps the code in a component and turns the refetch loop into a distractor.

options: Flips the label between ON and OFF on every click
Shows ON after the first click and stays there
Flips the label only when the parent re-renders
Shows OFF forever, because on is false in the handler
rewrite.hint: The updater is handed the current value rather than reading on from this render. Follow what it returns on the second click.
rewrite.explanation: Each click calls setOn(o => !o); React passes the latest stored value in as o and stores its negation, so the state alternates and the label follows it. setOn(!on) would also work here, but it reads the snapshot from the render that created the handler, which breaks as soon as two updates queue in one event. Nothing in the component depends on its parent, so the parent never enters into it.

rationale: Correct and clear, but it sits two bands below its level and three of its options are unusable, so as written it is free marks in a mastery set. The rewrite gives it one thing worth reasoning about, the functional updater, and it then clears both gates without pretending to be advanced.

objective: Read an effect that schedules a timeout and clears it on cleanup, and identify it as a debounce.
defects: 'runs cb immediately', 'an infinite loop' and 'an error' are throwaway options, and the automated flag is right that the key is the only descriptive one
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
the explanation names the pattern but not the role of the dependency, which is what makes it a debounce rather than a one-shot delay

options: Calls cb 500ms after the last change to cb
Calls cb immediately and again every 500ms
Calls cb 500ms after mount and never again
Calls cb on every render, 500ms behind
rewrite.hint: The cleanup runs before the effect runs again. Ask what happens to the pending timeout each time cb changes.
rewrite.explanation: Whenever cb changes, React runs the cleanup first, cancelling the timeout that was still pending, and then schedules a new one, so cb only ever runs once cb has stopped changing for 500ms: that is a debounce. With an empty dependency array the same code would fire once, 500ms after mount, and never restart. The cleanup is also what keeps it safe on unmount, since a cancelled timeout cannot call into a component that is gone.

rationale: A genuine mastery item: dependency-driven cleanup is the mechanism behind every debounce hook, and the key is right. The rewrite makes all four options timing behaviours, so the learner has to reason about the cleanup instead of eliminating nonsense.
evidence: node: React 19.2.8 with the delay shortened to 30ms, two cb changes 10ms apart produced 0 calls, and one call landed after the value settled for 45ms
node: unmounting before the timer fired produced no further call, so the cleanup cancelled it

objective: Know when a useMemo value recomputes: when one of its listed dependencies changes.
defects: 'never' and 'on unmount' are throwaway options
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
explanation restates the rule without saying how dependencies are compared, which is what decides whether a memo works in practice

options: When a or b changes between renders
On every render, since the arrow is recreated
Only on the first render, then never again
Whenever any state in the component changes
rewrite.hint: React stores the last result next to the last dependency values. Ask what it compares before deciding to run expensive again.
rewrite.explanation: useMemo keeps the value alongside the dependency array and compares each entry with Object.is on the next render; when they all match it hands back the stored value and never calls expensive. The inline arrow really is created on every render, but React does not call it unless a dependency changed. The trap is a dependency that is itself a new object or array each render, since it always compares as different and the memo then costs more than it saves.

rationale: Correctly keyed and the better of the two useMemo items, since expensive(a, b) with two dependencies justifies the memo that rm-react-195's cheap map does not. Only the two dead options, the filler hint and the thin explanation needed work.
